utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, we have a slightly larger component than normal today. I'm Tom Hannis along with Gerard Dobbyn; Case Manager, Crispian Smith; and one of our interns, Marina Vilova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I hope that today I'm going to be luckier than yesterday. Aleksandar Aleksic representing Mr. Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we are advised that your witness is available to begin, but before he is brought into the courtroom, are there any other matters which we should address?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I have to return back to the issue of disclosure under the Rule 66(B). If you remember, Your Honours, I will briefly just summarise. The decision of the Trial Chamber concerning the Rule 66(B) disclosure in -- with the previous witness, Mr. Bjelosevic, was that -- that the Defence did not provide enough specificity for the Office of the Prosecution to comply with, with our request which was made in January. Immediately after the ruling, we provided a request, a specified request in accordance with the Rule 66(B). The Office of the Prosecutor informed us that they will not comply with our request. We then filed a motion to comply, a motion to -- to compel -- sorry, motion to compel the Office of the Prosecution to compel with our 66(B) request. As Your Honours informed us, the matter is still pending before the Trial Chamber. When I brought it up on Monday this week, we were informed about that. Immediately after that, we again requested from the Office of the Prosecutor the documentation specifically connected to the witness which is about to enter the court. Now, on Tuesday we received the response from the Office of the Prosecutor that the Prosecution disclosed to us all documents which, in their opinion, are Rule 68, and that they are not -- they are not going to disclose the 66(B), according to our request, before the decision of the Trial Chamber. Now, Your Honours, it really leaves us in a very, I must say awkward position, the Defence, because the rules are here. We did everything which we can in accordance with the rule. The matter is pending before the Trial Chamber and now we are about to get into new witness, another witness, and as I said, it's halfway through our case, and we still -- and we are, if I may say so, we are walking with a blindfold in this matter. That is the information I wanted to give to the Trial Chamber, and perhaps Mr. Hannis can, if he wants to respond, and then I can go to the second matter which Your Honours invited me to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have a comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the request regarding this witness was for anything addressed to him or signed by him in 1992. We got that a couple of days ago. I see by the list of exhibits on the Defence list that they have a number of items signed by this witness which we didn't have in our collection, so obviously they have had access to some materials that we don't know, we don't have, and those kind of materials addressed to Mr. Andan or sent by Mr. Andan in the MUP in 1992 are certainly available to them through the state authorities, and the motion is pending. We are awaiting your ruling. If you direct us to comply with that request, we'll obviously do that, but I don't know if we have anything that they don't already have because we haven't gone to check that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the exchange between counsel just now illustrates the -- what is likely to happen with this witness and, indeed, for the future. As both counsel have said, you are awaiting the ruling of the Chamber on this matter which has been the subject of a formal motion by counsel for the accused, Stanisic. The issues raised by that motion are notwithstanding the experience and jurisprudence of the Tribunal over the years of its existence, such as that the matter is -- the basic issue is yet in a state of refinement, and that is one of the reasons why the decision of the Chamber has not been as speedily produced as counsel may have anticipated. The net result of all of this is that, as has happened up to this point, and as I said earlier, is likely to continue to happen -- is that such objections, applications, whatever, would be -- would have to be addressed as and when they arise on an issue-by-issue basis with various documents. There is no way of short-circuiting that, what everybody fears is going to be a -- could be a time-consuming process. But to come back to what I said earlier, the fact that despite the jurisprudence over the years, this is still a matter for disputation, means that the nature of the applications that tend to be made are ones that, particularly in the adversarial system, counsel are not going to see eye to eye, and the Chamber is going to have to, in exercise of its responsibility to deal with these matters as the trial progresses, deal with them as and when they arise. That's probably not a satisfactorily explanation at this point for counsel, but the ruling, when it comes and which we expect to be -- I'm not going to make any promises, but which we expect to be soon, will seek to bring together the syncing and experience of the Tribunal up to this point on this, what is obviously going to remain in this trial and probably other trials, a contentious issue. Your second matter, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just a brief comment, Your Honours. The problem, as we see it, is that this goes into the very crucial fairness of the proceedings before this Trial Chamber in this case because, I'm sorry to bring that up again, but the provisions of the Rule 66(B) have nothing to do with our ability to gather the information from state institutions or anything like that. It is a strict obligation of the Office of the Prosecutor to disclose to us the materials which are in their possession upon our request, and that is what we did. Now, Your Honours, we -- as I said, we are not in a position to know what are the documents because the Office of the Prosecutor does not want to disclose them to us upon our request. So that brings us to the point where we are not able to discuss with our witnesses a documentation which might be produced in the trial, and I think that goes to the very fairness of the proceedings before this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again you have put your finger on one of the reasons why this matter is not as straightforward as it might have first appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I wanted to add that in case, the Defence has access to the witness who certainly would be in a position to assist with identifying what documents he might have signed in 1992 and which ones he might have received and places to find those, and maybe even assisted the Defence in making more specific requests to us for a particular kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The second matter Your Honours invited us yesterday at the end of the session was about the -- our proofing note and the reference made to -- under point 18. And, Your Honours, I agree that on the face of it a number of matters which I provided in the proofing note in -- under 18 are not directly relevant for the issues in this case. However, all these issues are very, extremely important and relevant for the credibility of the witness because, as Your Honours will hear, the witness -- the witness's life has been full of ups and downs, and on a number of occasions, the witness was -- was sacked from his duties and work due to the allegations made by former ICTY Prosecutor, the high representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, therefore, I think that in this case, in these specific circumstances, the -- his credibility will be an issue which will be explored by the Office of the Prosecutor, and for these reasons we think that the matters which I stated in -- under number 18 of the proofing note are very important for establishing his credibility. That is the reason why we intend to lead the evidence on that particular issue shortly, as short as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. I had written to Mr. Zecevic about this and indicating to him my understanding from my experience and my practice in my jurisdiction. And the general rule is that when you present a witness, you are not permitted to introduce evidence basically to bolster the credibility of your witness unless and until his credibility has been attacked. Now, starting out on direct it hasn't been attacked because the Prosecution hasn't asked him a question, so it's something that may come up in redirect if the Prosecution attacks his credibility. On the other hand, if this evidence is being sought to undermine his credibility for some reason, well, then that's the Defence impeaching their own witness, and we say that's not a proper thing do in direct examination either. So for us, it's partly a matter of timing and only after, if it happens, that the Prosecution raises questions or attacks his credibility on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I confess that coming from a common law background, my instinctual reaction was just as Mr. Hannis has indicated, but I'm open [Realtime transcript read in error "hope"] to being persuaded, I suppose, that there may be room for the Defence -- sorry, for the calling party, in this case the Defence, reasonably anticipating a challenge that is likely to be made to lay the foundation. But, for the moment, I'm content to say nothing further and let's see how that develops.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So would the usher please escort the witness into court. I see that the transcript records me as saying that "I hope to be persuaded." What I think I said is that "I'm open to being persuaded." Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Would you please make the solemn declaration that's on the card the usher has handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And from your responses to me thus far, I assume that you are hearing me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we thank you for coming to assist the Tribunal by giving -- by agreeing to give evidence as a witness. And I would begin by asking you your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dragomir Andan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession, or what was your profession and what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have graduated from the faculty of political sciences. I spent all my career in the police. My ethnicity is Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your date of birth, sir, is when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 12th of April, 1951, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in any of the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have been called by the Defence of the first named accused in this indictment, Mr. Stanisic. And counsel for Mr. Stanisic, who is at your left, would begin by asking you questions, following which the counsel for the Prosecution, which is on the opposite side, on your right, would have an opportunity to ask questions of you. But before that, counsel for Mr. Stanisic's co-accused would also have an opportunities to ask questions. There will then be an opportunity for re-examination by the counsel calling you, and after that, or, indeed, at any intermediate stage, the members of the Bench may have questions of you. The time that has been indicated by counsel is that counsel calling you expects that they would require 20 hours to examine you. Counsel for the co-accused has indicated an hour, and counsel for the Prosecution has indicated themselves about 20 hours in cross-examination. Because the courtroom space is shared with other trials, the court sits either in morning sessions or afternoon sessions. For the time being, and probably for the duration of your testimony, we will be in morning sessions which begin at 9.00 and the Court rises at 1.45 to make room for another trial. However, that is not a continuous sitting. For technical reasons having to do with the recording of the proceedings, the sessions, the day's sitting is divided into sessions of not more than 90 minutes. This allows -- and the break is usually for 20 minutes which allows the necessary technical adjustments to be made but also provides for the convenience of witnesses and, indeed, counsel and everybody else concerned. But notwithstanding those fixed periods, if for any other reason you need to take a break, and we were advised that you, yourself, have been suffering from certain minor issues having to deal with the atmosphere in The Hague, we would -- you would notify us and we would, of course, accommodate you. When you came in, the first thing that happened was that the usher had you read the solemn declaration. This imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony to this Tribunal which is empowered under the statute which created it to impose severe penalties if you give false or misleading testimony. And at the beginning of every day's sitting, you would be reminded of that solemn declaration. If you have no questions of the Bench by way of general -- anything else that we should -- could explain to you, I would invite counsel for Mr. Stanisic to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, we heard that you were born in Sarajevo in 1951. Can you tell me, what is your family situation now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I come from a worker's family. My father took part in the Second World War, and at the end of it, he was the non-commissioned officer. His first and last post was in Sarajevo, where I was born. My father died in 1954. My mother, my sister and I were left alone. Four years later -- maybe I should first mention that my mother was 24 years old when my father died. Four years later, she married again, a Croat, called Trpimir Sepcic. From that second marriage, I have a brother and a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, are you married? Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I am married. I have two sons, Milos and Ivan. Milos is 32. He graduated at business school. Ivan is 28. He is a lawyer. My wife is an economist and we've been married since 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you said that you spent your whole career in the police. When did you commence your employment in the Ministry of the Interior which used to be called the Secretariat of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It used to be called the Republican Ministry of Interior. I commenced working there in March 1976 in the state security department which was the secret police of the then state. There was public security and state security, and I began working in the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you begin working?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: In the state security in Sarajevo. It had its zones and I was in the security centre Sarajevo. That service covered all the municipalities in Sarajevo. I don't know exactly what was the number of the Sarajevo municipalities at that time. I think it was around 20 municipalities. There was, of course, also more structured hierarchy about which I could maybe talk later in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to speak a little bit slower because of the interpreters. Could you tell me what functions did you perform in the Ministry of the Interior in the Socialist Republic of BiH. Could you tell us what time-periods and what they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: In 1983, we were about to complete the preparations for the Olympic games in Sarajevo that were held in 1984. By is decision by the minister and the undersecretary for the state security of BiH, a number of us operatives in the state security were transferred to the public security service. I was appointed the commander of police station in Novo Sarajevo. That was the largest police station in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. I performed that function until 1986. After which, because of a number of problems in the Stari Grad municipality, I was appointed by the decision of the ministry to the post of the chief of the station which I performed until 1990. My mandate lasted for four years, and after that I was transferred to the Ministry of the Interior to the police administration where I was an inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify one thing. The municipality that you mentioned, Stari Grad, is it one of the Sarajevo municipalities and in which part of town is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: That's one of the municipalities in Sarajevo. It's the oldest municipality in Sarajevo. It comprises Bascarsija where the population was predominantly Muslim, around 97 [Realtime transcript read in error "90"] per cent of Muslims; 2 percent of Serbs; and 1 per cent of others. So it's the oldest municipality in the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you said 97 per cent Muslims, we see a different number in the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I said 97 per cent Muslims, 2 per cent Serbs and 1 per cent others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, in 1990, in the BiH MUP, which function did you perform at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I was senior inspector 1st class at the time. But today in Republika Srpska, it would be called chief inspector of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just explain the hierarchy. If we look at the senior inspector 1st class, who was above you in the hierarchy in your administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: My immediate superior was chief of the department, and after that assistant minister for police work or, later on, undersecretary for police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The conflicts in April and May 1992, where were you when the hostilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina broke out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in April 1992, I was senior inspector 1st class. So from 1990 until the beginning of the war, I performed the same function.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did you transfer to the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I should make a short introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, just give us the dates and then we are going to go into details later on during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I remained in Sarajevo until the second half of May 1992, and then I went to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Until when did you remain working in the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I worked there until the second half of August 1992 and then I was transferred to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the VRS and what rank did you have in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Since I graduated from the reserve officer school in Zadar and was accorded the rank of 1st lieutenant, later on I was promoted to the lieutenant, I entered the VRS as a captain and I left the VRS at the end of the war as the reserve major. I remained in the army until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you said that your rank was reserve major at the end?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when did you return to work in the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I was officially appointed on the 1st of January, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What did you do between 1996 when you left the VRS and the 1st of January, 2000?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, or maybe luckily for me, I performed various jobs. For awhile I was in the Belgrade harbour carrying sacks from truck to truck. Later on, I worked at the large fruit market and vegetable market. Later on, I worked for some friends who transported tomatoes and cucumbers from Greece. So I would sell those things from 5.30 in the morning until 4.00 p.m. I was even a waiter and a manage manager of a cafe in Herceg Novi for awhile. I think it was in 1999. So I did everything but what I was qualified for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for you to return to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, and when did you start discussions in that direction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, that was, practically speaking, half of my career. I needed another 20 years before I could retire, and I could not retire working in the jobs that I did. So when I considered all the factors, I concluded that it would be best for me if I returned to the Ministry of the Interior to work on the jobs that I worked on for a number of years. In 1999, I decided to get in touch with the then minister of the interior Sredoje Jovic [phoen], I wanted to speak to him about my possibly of my return to the Ministry of the Interior. We had a conversation sometime in December 1999. The minister told me that they are short of personnel, especially of personnel of my qualifications. So he offered me to work as an inspector in the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. So at the time I felt that this could give me some sort of security, financial security and also other forms of security, and that's why I decided to commence working again in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After your return to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, you said that you returned to the position of an inspector in the ministry. What were your other functions in the Ministry of Republika Srpska, and could you give us the time-periods?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I did not stay for long on the post of inspector, maybe six months in total. I was then promoted to the chief of the general police work department. The structure of the police has the department for general police work and the department for traffic police, and there are two chiefs. I was one of the chiefs. So as I said, after six months I was promoted to the post of the chief of general police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The police administration, is that something that relates to what we normally call uniform police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: There are two administrations in the ministry: The crime police administration, they wear civilian clothes; and the police administration, they wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If my math is correct, sometime around mid-2000 you became chief of this general police, if I can call them that. How much time did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I will kindly ask you not to take my word for dates because I'm very bad with dates. I have to say that this promotion of mine came after the Bosniaks first came to Srebrenica in an organised fashion, so the minister made a decision appointing me chief of security for that event. Given the political tensions involved in the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was entrusted with this very difficult task of organising the unhindered arrival of Bosnians in Srebrenica so that they honour their dead for the first time, that they visit the site where the war crime had been committed and that they safely return to the Federation. Most fortunately, this proved to be a job well done and I think that that is when my promotion came. As for the duty of chief of general police, I think I remained in that position sometime until 2003, and then from that post I was transferred to the post of inspector in Prijedor, the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How shall I put this, this transfer from the post of chief of general police and the MUP of Republika Srpska to the post of inspector in Prijedor, was this a promotion or was it something different?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: For me, that was degradation. I don't know if we have enough time for me to explain why that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, please, just in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: In the municipality of Sokolac, the then chief of the Security Services Centre, Zeljko Markovic, was killed. As chief of the general police department, I sent special police forces up there to search the terrain and to help in that first stage of the investigation. When we game up there to the funeral, I was informed that not everything was done in accordance with regulations and that certain segments had not been taken care of properly. I told Dragomir Jovicic, the then minister, that I did not agree with how part of the investigation had been initiated, and I told him what should be done in the next stage, first and foremost, to find the killer. The orders I received said that I would be head of the investigation team up there in Sokolac. On the next day, I left Banja Luka for Sokolac. Before I left, the minister told me to do my best to find the perpetrator, and then once we get that done, that I could choose my post within the Ministry of Interior. I said to him that it was my professional duty, first and foremost, to find the perpetrator and that I was not considering different posts at that time at all. We'd come half way to Travnik and I was told that the situation had changed and that I should go back. I'm an operative by nature. I called a few numbers and I learned that part of the political structures, especially from Sokolac, were not in favour of my coming to Sokolac to be in charge of the investigation. I also heard that they asked the Ministry of the Interior that I return. As a matter of fact, they said that they would not guarantee my safety there. That irritated me terribly. When I returned to Banja Luka, I said everything that I've said to you just now. I said all of that to the minister, and I said, Why did you not let me go up there? And if someone even started behaving in an offensive manner, you would know what this was all about. I think that right now you don't want to bring the investigation to an end and you don't really want to find the perpetrator. Quite simply, there was no answer. I was most dissatisfied with that kind of behaviour, and a few days after that in a weekly paper in Banja Luka which is called "Reporter [phoen]," I gave an interview where I explained everything that had happened and how work is being done in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood this correctly, the outcome of this interview was your transfer to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do in Prijedor and for how long?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I worked in the field of general crime. I think that I spent five or six months there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: What came then was a sudden call. It was sudden for me, at least. It was the minister of the interior, Mr. Djeric, who called me to come to Banja Luka to see him at his office to talk about my transfer. Truth to tell, I was surprised by the offer that was made. After a series of problems and after all the problems that had accumulated in the security centre of East Sarajevo, he was offering that centre to me. That is to say, he wanted to have me transferred to become chief of the CSB Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I forget, I just wanted to request that counsel clarify which Mr. Djeric it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which Mr. Djeric you are referring to, we know of Mr. Djeric who was prime minister of the government of Republika Srpska in 1992, so could you tell us who this Mr. Djeric is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It is Zoran Djeric. I don't know whether he is closely related to the former prime minister, but this is Zoran Djeric, who is now vice-president of the PDP political party, the party of Mladen Jovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So these are two different people, right, the Zoran Djeric that you are speaking about and the prime minister of Republika Srpska from 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, these are two different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that, you became chief of the CSB of Istocno Sarajevo, East Sarajevo, how much time did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I was there until January 2005, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in the beginning of January 2005?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I received a call from the office of the president of the republic, Mr. Dragan Cavic. Again, I'm saying please don't take my word for the date. I know that it was 2005. I know that one morning or one day at 11.00 I was supposed to come to his office for a meeting. Since hierarchy is in my blood, I immediately told the minister of the interior that the president of the republic has invited me to come, and he said that I should go and that he would be there as well. In the office of the president, I found Mr. Paddy Ashdown, Mr. Cavic and Mr. Matijasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, you mentioned three names, could you please tell us who held which position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Mr. Paddy Ashdown at the time was high representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I think that the spelling of Paddy Ashdown is different from what the transcript reflects right now. It's spelled with a double D. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Cavic was president of the Republika Srpska at the time. And Mr. Darko Matijasevic was minister of the interior of the MUP of Republika Srpska. Of course, I addressed the president of the republic and I said that I was hereby reporting. I was told that after a series of analyses and conversations, I was selected to be the person who would inter alia be in charge of the work that has to do with The Hague Tribunal. So my role was, at least that is what I was told, and later on that came to fruition, that in the forthcoming period I would become director of the police in the MUP of Republika Srpska and that our primary task was the arrest and prosecution of all persons that are fugitives and are wanted by The Hague Tribunal. Perhaps this was preceded by yet another event. While I was chief of the CSB of East Sarajevo, I received intelligence to the effect that in the area of Visegrad there are two or three mass graves where Muslims were buried. We informed a person by the name of Don King, I believe, about that. He is an investigator and a representative of The Hague Tribunal in Sarajevo. We agreed to investigate all three mass graves and to provide this documentation to them. In order to be able to do that properly, we informed the Prosecutor about that as well, we established an on-site investigation team and we investigated these three mass graves where Bosniaks had been buried. The call came after all of that. Probably the assessment was that I did not want to have any crimes concealed, rather I wanted things to be resolved as soon as possible. When I spoke to the president and the minister at the time, Mr. Paddy Ashdown said that if Republika Srpska does not apprehend persons wanted by The Hague Tribunal by April 2005 there will be no Republika Srpska. First of all, I was a bit perplexed at that point in time, but I did agree, I said that I would do my very best to have all of this resolved, that I would spare no effort, as far as my own efforts were concerned and those of my co-workers, and that I would embark upon this task very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we now briefly move into private session just for a few questions that I have to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your capacity of director of police of Republika Srpska, did you hand in the indictment to Mr. Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, and by your leave, I would explain how I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just the main details, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that necessary, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have an explanation as to the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can take his earphones off. Your Honours, I believe it is very important for the Trial Chamber and everybody to understand the attitude of Mr. Stanisic and the attitude of his towards the indictment that he is standing trial at this point now. And this is the witness who can give us details of what was said, what was done, and what was the -- what was the reaction of Mr. Stanisic to the indictment that he received on that point. I think, and I'm -- I firmly believe it is important for the Trial Chamber to hear this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, there's a another source of that evidence available. In addition, Mr. Stanisic gave a suspect interview to the OTP for five or six days which is in evidence and there's, I say, ample sufficient -- of his attitude contained therein. The fact that he may have said something to this witness, and this witness handed him the indictment in 1994, is not going take you very far. It's an, I say it's an attempt to get in self-serving evidence of the accused without the accused having to take the stand and being cross-examined. In addition, this is not the situation where a policeman is coming to court and testifying about having arrived at the murder scene, talked to the accused who said, Oh my God, I'm sorry I did it. It's not in the nature of an excited utterance. In 1994, there's quite a likelihood that Mr. Stanisic was aware that something was in the works and so the value of any utterance he made at that time is greatly reduced because it's not in the nature of -- in common law, we talk about as excited utterances which are treated as exceptions to hearsay because there's a general opinion that they are more reliable. That's not the circumstances here. And for that reason, I would object and ask you not to permit this as its not relevant, and if it is relevant, it has no weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I agree with the submissions that have been made by Mr. Hannis, Mr. Zecevic, and I don't know that I could improve on his language, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, we will leave this issue aside, given that the Chamber decided that they don't need to hear your evidence on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if you are about to move on to something else, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we rise, Mr. Andan, I would point this out to you, you've indicated before that you haven't previously testified, and we appreciate that a person who comes as a witness has a story to tell with a whole background which he is anxious to get out. But in order for evidence to be manageable in this Tribunal as with any courtroom, the role that counsel plays is that counsel knows what he has to establish, and therefore asks questions directed to what he seeks to do. So therefore, it is important for a witness to listen to counsel's question and answer the question, rather than volunteering excess information. So if you would bear that in mind when we resume, we would be able to move ahead much more swiftly. Thank you. We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We apologise for taking the Bench later than we had intended to, but it would be appreciated that judges try to use the breaks to get rid of some of the pressing matters which are always before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, tell me, please, how long did you remain the director of police of Republika Srpska? How long did you remain in that post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think until May of 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you removed from that position on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't removed. I resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the reason for your resignation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Prime minister of the RS government, Milorad Dodik, received a letter sent by Ms. Carla del Ponte in which she said that I was part of the organised crime ring and that such a person should not perform or should not serve at such a high position in Republika Srpska. After that letter, I had a conversation with Mr. Dodik and I asked that an investigation be instituted after which I would resign, and he said that I should resign first, following which I could be moved to another position within the ministry, following which I could take legal measures to investigate the claims made by Mrs. del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what position were you appointed next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: A compromise was found. I was appointed deputy chief of police education administration in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for the other suggestion made to you, to undertake legal steps in order to ascertain the truthfulness of allegations contained in that letter, did you do anything about that, and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: The letter of Mrs. del Ponte contained the assertion that she has certain information, some of which was confirmed by Vinzenzo Copola, the chief of European police in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wrote to Mr. Copola first and I asked him it that if he has any incriminations related to Dragomir Andan that he should forward them to the Prosecutor's Office, and I am ready to appear before any court in relation to any act of mine. In the mean time, I believe Mrs. del Ponte was replaced. I wrote a similar letter to Mr. Serge Brammertz and I requested the state prosecutor's office of the BiH to forward all allegation of Mrs. Del Ponte to any court in Bosnia-Herzegovina before which I would then be ready to appear if I really committed a criminal offence. I received no answer to any of those letters. There was no other legal avenue open for me. You are well aware of the fact that various international structures such as the office of high representatives are institutions against which no legal proceedings can be instigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you undertake any measures before the state prosecutor's office of BiH in relation to this matter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, after I wrote the two letters, I spoke on the phone requesting to be received by Mr. Marinko Jurcevic in the state Prosecutor's Office. Mr. Jurcevic received me. Present was also his deputy, Barasin, and chief in charge of war crimes, whose name I think is Mr. Senduk [phoen]. I requested them to provide me some explanations, and I asked Mr. Jurcevic to detain me on the very day that I arrived in Sarajevo. I wanted the full investigation be conducted, and if anything is found against me that I should be immediately indicted; and if not, I wanted them to issue some sort of certificates stating that the state Prosecutor office is not conducting any sort of proceedings against me. Mr. Jurcevic told me, either consciously or unconsciously, that there is no investigation any sort of proceedings against me in their office but the problem lies in the OHR.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you perform the duty of assistant for police education in the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It wasn't assistant, it was deputy chief of administration. I remained on that post until the 10th of July, 2007. Then Mr. Lajcak, the high representative, made a decision banning me from work in all organs of -- in all government organs. My personal documents were taken from me, ID and passport, and I was precluded from crossing the state border. That decision was taken on 10th of July, 2007. In the disposition of the decision they wrote that I am a part of the support network for Radovan Karadzic and that I'm financing him. I have a copy of that decision and, of course, you also have a copy of that decision here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that decision?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I requested to be received by the relevant official of the OHR because I was seeking answers. Unfortunately, I was never received by Mr. Lajcak. However, I was received by his deputy on a number of he occasions, Mr. Gregor Jani [phoen]. In the first conversation, I requested to be retired. I asked them, What do you think, how am I going to live? And they told me, Well, that's your problem, but you cannot be retired. So in addition to all the measures undertaken against me, I was precluded from retiring, although taken together with the war time, I had about 42 years of pensionable years. This was the most difficult period of my life. If necessary, I can go into more details, but this is a very difficult and painful subject for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you fired from the Ministry of the Interior after that decision made by the high representative on the 10th of July, 2007?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I received the decision on the 10th of July. On the 11th of July, in the morning, 9.00 in the morning, I was called by the minister of interior of Republika Srpska, Mr. Cargo and he handed me the decision terminating my employment. I used all legal avenues available to me in Bosnia and Herzegovina against that decision, from the lower court to the highest instance which is the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, all of them declared lack of jurisdiction in any sort of dispute involving the Office of High Representative. I was told that I could maybe go before the human rights court in Strasbourg, which I did. In the meantime, I addressed the high representatives, all of them between Miroslav Lajcak and Mr. Insk [phoen]. I probably wrote to them around 20 times asking for various things. First of all, I wanted them to permit me to visit my family in Belgrade, for Christmas, for Easter and for New Year. I was not permitted to do that. So although I didn't even have an apartment there, and I still don't have an apartment there, which means that I am a tenant. I had to rent an apartment. I was not permitted to visit my family even during most important holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The situation that arose on the 10th of July, 2007, how long did it last? How long did you have this particular status?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: After I've exhausted all legal possibilities that I knew of, finding myself in a completely helpless situation, last year in September I decided to undertake a radical move. I began a hunger strike. I did that in front of the building of the Office of High Representative in Banja Luka. I was on hunger strike for 22 days until I was taken to a hospital and treated. I spent three or four days in hospital. After that, I received another 15 intervenous treatments, and shortly after that, I received an information from the Office of High Representative, although it was mostly media that I saw it, that I and another 13 persons were to receive the personal documents that they would be allowed to cross the state border, and after that in the conversation with the representatives of the Office of High Representatives, I asked whether I would be allowed to retire. My request was granted. So, all in all, I told you already that you shouldn't really rely on me for precise dates, but it all ended sometime in April last year. This was the first measure imposed on me. The second measure, and that is the ban on employment in all government organs, is still in effect, and I don't know how long it is going to remain in effect. During all this time, no Prosecutor in Bosnia and Herzegovina ever instigated any proceedings against me and it has never been proved that I was part of the support network for Radovan Karadzic. When he was transferred to The Hague Tribunal, I was then hand a new decision alleging that I was part of the support network for Ratko Mladic and Goran Hadzic. I do not understand any of those two decisions, but these are the facts and these are the things that I have to reckon with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you give any interviews to the Prosecutor's Office of this Tribunal, and if so, how many times and when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think I spoke to them twice, I don't know the names of persons involved, and it's probably not important. Once we spoke about Brcko. We spoke in Brcko. I don't know exactly in which offices. And the second interview was in 2006 or 2007 in the Tribunal offices in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you remember whether there were -- whether you were interviewed the Tribunal investigators as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think that I was told quite openly during the second interview that I was not a suspect. And as for the first interview in Brcko, my understanding was that it was some sort of almost a friendly conversation. The interview in Banja Luka was a bit more serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the relevant period now. Period relevant for these proceedings. Until which year were you the chief of the public security station Stari Grad in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I was the chief there from 1986 until 2000. Excuse me, excuse me, 1986 until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were the chief of the public security station of Stari Grad in Sarajevo, and from that position you were transferred to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH. Why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: In 1986, I was appointed to the position of the chief pursuant to the order by the then minister of the interior, Dusko Zgonjanin. The reason was the fact that that particular station had the worst performance in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were many problems in that station and I was told to bring some order into the station. Every year there was some sort of league table published for the police stations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. After two years, we were in fifth place, and shortly thereafter, in the second place, which means that the situation was rather stable. And I thought that there were fortuitous conditions to continue in that direction. In 1990, there were also changes at the very top of the Ministry of the Interior. Mr. Dusko Zgonjanin left his post. I think he was retired. He was replaced by Muhamed Besic. Mr. Besic invited me to his office. Before my mandate was over, at the time I expected that I was going to remain on the duty for another mandate, I was told that essentially they were satisfied with my work, but that it would be inappropriate for me, a Serb, to be the chief of police station in the territory with 97 per cent of Muslims. I was told that they were not going to extend my mandate and that I could choose whether I wanted to go to the crime police or general police in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They thought that that was an appropriate solution for me. I accepted their offer in 1990 and I was transferred, or I returned to the Ministry of the Interior, and I accepted the post of inspector in the general police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What were your specific duties in -- on the post of inspector in the Ministry of the Interior of Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, beginning in 1990?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Inspectors were in charge of various security centres. My duties at the time were to follow and direct the work in Eastern Herzegovina. I mean by that, the police stations in Eastern Herzegovina. At the time the security centre in Trebinje had not been established because Trebinje was under Mostar at the time. But another colleague of mine and I divided the Security Services Centre in Mostar into two parts, so I followed the events in the Eastern Herzegovina and he followed the events in Western Herzegovina. We were mainly involved in supervisory inspection. We followed and directed the work of police stations as part of the organs of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say supervisory inspection, following and directing, can you give us a brief explanation of those duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: First of all, we would go into the field and it was our duty to check the legality of work of police stations, as well as the general situation with law and order. Part of our duties pertained to the situation in traffic and the general situation related to crime as far as police is involved in following the crime. Part of our duties involved the civil situation and the relation of people in uniform towards, as we used to say then, working people and citizens, as well as relations between superiors and inferiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As we have heard, you started working on that in 1990. I would appreciate it if you would tell us what your conclusion would be with regard to what the situation was like in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the whole.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: After the first multi-party elections, the first ones since 1945, and the rather stable political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina when the political parties that formed the government won the election in the Ministry of the Interior itself, the situation became more complex. This primarily relates to personnel, Serb, Muslims, and Croats who were verified personnel, as it were, and successfully carried out their duties. Once the new political structure came to head Bosnia-Herzegovina, personnel changes took place. What worried us terribly was the fact that these tried and tested people who had been in the service for over 20 years were being replaced by individuals who we knew only sporadically or were not in the service at all before that. A few of us professionals came to the conclusion that professionalism no longer mattered, that it was party affiliation that did in order to please this new political structure and in this way people got certain jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time were instructive dispatches of the MUP acted upon properly in accordance with the law? And you as an inspector and your colleagues, did you check whether these instructive dispatches of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina were indeed being acted upon in the territory that you visited?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the town of Ljubuski is it in Eastern Herzegovina? And in this period between 1990 and 1992, that is, did you visit the public security station in Ljubuski, and, if so, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I was instructed by Mr. Avdo Hebib, chief of administration, to go to Ljubuski because the commander of the police station who had been there was replaced and an ethnic Muslim was supposed to be appointed to that position. So I was supposed to be present during the hand-over of duty, and for awhile I was supposed to stay there and help this new commander of the police station. To my surprise, that was the first case of this kind, I was accorded full hospitality there. But if you will allow me, with all due apologies to the Trial Chamber, I will directly quote what was said, that a Turk would never become the chief of the public security station in Ljubusk i, that I can have lunch there, that I can have a cup of coffee and go back to Sarajevo, and that I'm perfectly free to report to my superiors in Sarajevo, that they were unwilling to accept that kind of decision in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Tell us, the chief of this public security station was of what ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The town of Ljubuski, is it predominantly populated by Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: As far as I know, the majority were Croats, perhaps about 80 per cent, and 20 per cent were Muslims. I think that there was no Serb population in that area, and it is a municipality that is in Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember approximately when this happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think that it was in 1991. As a matter of fact, the second half of September, I think, because I know that it was the grape harvesting season and that there was fruit in abundance there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had just started answering and I interrupted you. You were saying as you went back to Sarajevo and so on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: As I was getting out of town, out of Ljubuski that is, on the right-hand side there is, probably to this day, a football stadium. At that stadium we then saw about 2- to 300 young men there, that would be my estimate. They were wearing camouflage trousers and black shirts with the checkerboard sign, and they were exercising. Since this is close to the road where we were passing, we could clearly see next to the checkerboard sign or emblem on the left sleeve it clearly said HOS. That was my first encounter with a paramilitary structure. That is what I then saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Hebib, your chief, had sent you there, the chief of your administration that is, did you report back to Mr. Hebib about this situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It was our duty to report every time we went out into the field and when we came back to headquarters. Of course I wrote up an Official Note about everything that I saw at the Ljubuski stadium. I forwarded that and there were no reactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, Mr. Andan, at the time when you were senior inspector 1st class in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who did you share an office with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Enver Dupovac was my colleague. He held the same rank as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And your direct superior was Avdo Hebib, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, the chief. The chief of the administration was Avdo Hebib, and Cedo Kljajic was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was Mr. Avdo Hebib a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Mr. Avdo Hebib worked at the infirmary of the republican MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a psychologist. For many years he had tried to come to work in the Ministry of the Interior. He had a problem there because his father, at least according to the checks that we ran in the secret police at the time, was a member of the so-called Handzar Divisions during the Second World War. He had been declared a war criminal and, as such, Avdo was not eligible, according to the criteria that were in place at the time, to work in the Ministry of the Interior. As for this wish of his to be transferred to the Ministry of the Interior, he managed to have it fulfilled when the SDA and other political parties came to power. He was immediately appointed assistant minister or undersecretary for police affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, at the time what kind of personnel policy was conducted in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think that the personnel policy that was pursued was an unprincipled one, especially as far as Bosniak personnel were concerned. I'm going to give you two examples. As chief of the public security station, I initiated misdemeanour and criminal proceedings against a policeman. His employment had been terminated by a decision of the ministry and I don't know what the punished meted out was for the offences that he had committed. When a multi-party system was introduced in Bosnia-Herzegovina, one morning this policeman showed up at the entrance of the republican SUP and he was in charge of allowing people to enter the building. The second example was Celo Bajramovic, the deceased Celo Bajramovic by now. In 2003, we arrested him while I worked in Novo Sarajevo. He was convicted to 14 years in prison, which was a precedent in terms of imprisonment policy at the time because due to general crime he was convicted to 14 years in prison. One morning as I was setting out to work, there was an automobile that had been turned upside-down in the street, and I asked the policeman, Who did this? And he said, Don't ask. This is a disaster. And I said, Why disaster? And he said, Bajramovic took out his official ID and did that and said do whatever you want with the car. This is just a small example of what was going on in that year in 1991 as far as personnel is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By way of an illustration, could the witness please be shown 1D247 -- 347, tab number 1. Your Honours, I have a binder of documents that has been prepared. Could I please have the assistance of the usher so that the witness could be given these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, first a question: What was the name of the then assistant minister for personnel affairs in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Before that, he was the manager of the Sarajevo brewery. His name is Ibro Selimovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this gentleman Hilmo Selimovic, at some point in time during 1991, was actually replaced by another individual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes. I think that he did not hold that position for a very long time. If I remember correctly, Mr. Mirsad Srebrenikovic replaced him, but, as far as I can remember, he came from Zagreb to replace him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this document, the document in front of you. It is signed, or rather, what is typewritten is "Secretary of the SDA, Hasan Cengic." This is communication of the Party of Democratic Action, and could you please give us your comment in respect of this document. What I'm specifically interested in is whether this document illustrates the situation that prevailed in the personnel service in the Ministry of the Interior of Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, fully. It fully illustrates the situation which came about once Jusuf Pusina came to the position of chief of police as well as Mirsad Srebrenikovic. The personnel policy became radicalised. While Selimovic was in his post as well as Avdo Hebib, they did take care of the long serving personnel who performed their duties in a lawful manner. Once Mr. Pusina and Mr. Srebrenikovic who was unknown to all of us, and later on we heard that he had come from Zagreb, and one of my colleagues started describing their policy as though we had been -- we had started appointing people who had just come from the mosque. I don't know whether Mr. Srebrenikovic used to work as a religious person or he worked in the religious department of the service in Zagreb, I'm not sure, but I know that he came from those kinds of circles. It is clear from this letter that the Party of Democratic Action had a direct influence over personnel policy and it instructed all security centres that the chief was to pursue a personnel policy that was in accordance with what the SDA wanted. The SJB personnel decisions also had to be approved by the SDA and the same principle applied at higher levels, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your previous answer when you quoted the comment of your colleagues concerning Mr. Srebrenikovic and his appointment, you gave us the name and the last name of that colleague of yours who said that -- however, it wasn't recorded in the transcript because you spoke quite quickly. Would you please give us your [as interpreted] name, who it was that uttered that comment and could you explain us who that person is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: That is Kemal Sabovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Kemal Sabovic was of which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak. He was of Muslim ethnicity. He used to work in the police administration, and he was chief of the general police department. He was a colleague of mine. Kemal Sabovic and I have known each other for almost 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you socialise, were you on friendly terms with Mr. Sabovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: He was the only person from the service that I socialised with after business hours. We would even visit each other in our homes. We were good friends and good family friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did he also work in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the police administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, we got to know each other back in 1983 at work when I was appointed chief of the police station in Novo Sarajevo. At that time he was the assistant to the municipal secretary for MUP. I then moved to Stari Grad municipality and he became an inspector in the republican MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us now go back to the personnel issues in the Ministry of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior. We discussed this document. Tell me, please, the other national political parties, and by that I'm referring to HDZ and the SDS, did they have a similar personnel policy similar to that of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And these other political parties, did they also appoint persons who were not up to the tasks that they were to fulfill in those posts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want document 65 ter 781D1, tab 1D, to be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, as far as I can see, the document that we still have on the screen is MFI'd. And so my question is whether you are putting this document to the witness as an attempt to have it de-MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for reminding me. Yes, I would like to have this document de-MFI'd at this point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, this is Exhibit 1D347.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document before you now is a dispatch from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina signed by the deputy minister, Vitomir Zepinic, dated 20th of February, 1992. Would you please give us your comment, if you can?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Practically in the same wing of the building of the republican MUP, in the administration there were all departments of the administration including the department for defence preparations. We were terribly surprised, if not shocked, when we learned of the content of this dispatch, namely that Mr. Jasarevic would take over the task of defence preparations. We thought that he was not competent for such an important post, that he was not up to it. He was assistant secretary or assistant chief in the public security station for the same matters. So this was a huge jump up from the level of the municipal secretariat up to the ministry level. This was an unprecedented jump in the history of the Ministry of the Interior, and this was yet another example that qualification, professional qualifications were not taken into account and that the only feature that was important was party affiliation. What was shocking for us is that he was supposed to be in charge of the entire reserve forces of the entire police in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In lower levels, each police station had its own reserve police force, and as the levels went up, the same rule applied and all of us who worked for the police administration -- was a huge chunk to bite for him and that this was a completely disastrous decision that was taken in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we" in the police administration, who do you have in mind specifically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It is probably difficult to describe this situation to anybody who was not in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. There were few people that one could speak openly to and tell them that a certain decision was not a good one, was not a proper one. In that period of time in 1992, there were already national split taking place between the employees. Even those who used to be friends during the socialist regime started splitting along the ethnic lines. One of the very few people that I could still talk at the time was Mr. Kemal Sabovic who completely shared my opinion concerning Mr. Jasarevic. Mr. Sabovic did not support any political party and this is why he was able to speak so freely to me. He was also not a favourite of the SDA, even though he was a Muslim. And this is why he probably felt he could speak his mind to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my only objection was it wasn't shown to Mr. Zepinic when he was here and it was his document. However, based on the witness's answers, it appears that this did actually happen and so I don't object to that. But I do object to using documents that could have been shown to the author when they were here before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D546, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, can I give another explanation concerning this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It is true that Mr. Zepinic signed this document. However, one has to bear in mind that political parties or representatives of political parties agreed who would be appointed to what post, and then this was just given to Zepinic to sign as something that had been drafted, to sign and implement. It's not that I'm trying to justify the actions of Zepinic, but this is how things were done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let me show you another document, 65 ter 822D1, tab 1C. Sir, this document pertains to the events of 29th of February and 1st of March, 1992, in Sarajevo and the subsequent barricades that appeared in the days to follow in the streets of Sarajevo. Would you please briefly explain to us what you know about these events and the barricades.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Do you want me to clarify the events of March 1st firstly and then move on to subsequent events?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First the events that took place on the 1st of March, and then the barricades.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: The intelligence that we had and also the information that I acquired later on clearly indicated that on the 1st of March in Bascarsija behind the old Orthodox church, a member of a wedding party was killed, a prominent member of a wedding party. And that this was the fuse that set alight the events that followed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The service of the interior affairs at the time basically obstructed the investigation aimed at finding the perpetrator and initiating prosecution. This mostly had to do with private checks and privately acquired information by way of which I learned that the murder was committed by Rasim Delalic [phoen], nicknamed Celo. What is completely incredible is that the then commander of the Stari Grad police station, who was the commander at the time when I was chief of that station, and his name was Ismet Dahic took him in the official business vehicle of MUP to Travnik and hid him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify this. This is the event which took place on the 1st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were chief of the public security station in Stari Grad until 1990?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you know, when did Ismet Dahic start working as commander of the public security station in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Given that at the time the ethnic composition was important, I represented the Serbian community, ethnically speaking, so it was natural that my first assistant would be of a Muslim ethnicity. I knew Dahic, he was head of the armoured unit within the special units of the then ministry. So I suggested to Grgisa Munac [phoen], I asked him to allow me to appoint him commander of the Stari Grad SJB, and he came to that post in late 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it was upon your recommendation that Ismet Dahic was appointed commander of the Stari Grad SJB in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It wasn't just him. Jusuf Pusina had also my recommendation and many others. Dahic was appointed commander of the Stari Grad SJB upon my recommendation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it because of this fact that you say now that you were surprised when you found out that Ismet Dahic used an official vehicle to transport the perpetrator of the crime committed on the 1st of March, 1992, to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, he did his job properly. He was a good commander of a police station. And I'm surprised that he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I see the time. Is it an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, that evening after the event at Bascarsija, were you called to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think it was the same evening. We received a call through the duty service in the Ministry of the Interior, I think at around midnight, to come to the Ministry of the Interior but we were not told what were the reasons. I was one of the people who came to the ministry in order to find out what this was about. We were told that we would be told the reasons when we appeared for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who told you the reasons and who attended the meeting in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, nobody told us any reasons. We were just shuffling our feet in the offices without knowing why we had to come there, and then at one moment one of the colleagues said Serbs had put up the barricades at the Vrbanja bridge and cut the city two halves, but there were no orders for us to undertake any activities. Sometimes toward the morning, somebody thought that it would be good to go to Bascarsija because the shops there open among the first shops in Sarajevo, so we simply wanted to see whether we could get some of our bread rolls and something else to eat. So a decision was made that Mr. Music, a colleague of mine, and I should go and bring some food. I would just like to say one more thing, Teufik Music is a colleague of mine who worked with me in both state security and public security. He lives in the Stari Grad municipality in the settlement called Vratnik. We went by car towards Bascarsija and we were stopped at the City Hall. The people who stopped us wore uniforms that we were unfamiliar with at the time. There were some people in civilian clothes and some people in uniform there. They all had long barrels. So of course we stopped the car. Both Teufik Music and I recognised one Sulejman, Suljo, Agic while I was the chief, who was a shift leader in the public security station in Stari Grad, so we exchanged a few words and they let us go. Teufik wanted to go up to Vratnik to pick up some things from his house and that's why we first went to Vratnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one detail. This Suljo Aic, was he an active policeman at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I could see, there were about six or seven of them and he was the only active policeman among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And who were the others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Some of them, two or three of them, wore uniforms of the reserve police force. I could easily recognise them because they wore winter uniforms made from heavy cloth. All the reserve members of the reserve police force in Bosnia and Herzegovina wore that kind of uniforms. And the remaining two or three people simply had leather jackets, jeans, military boots, and a rifle.
